title: PSPACE-completeness of resolution clause space
formal:
Is the following language \(\mathrm{ResClauseSpace}\) PSPACE-complete under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions?
\[\mathrm{ResClauseSpace}=\{\langle F,s\rangle:\ F\text{ has a general resolution refutation in clause space at most }s\}.\]
Here \(F\) is any finite CNF formula, with no fixed bound on input clause width, and \(s\ge0\) is an integer encoded in binary. A refutation starts with no stored clauses and may download an input clause, derive a resolvent or weakening of currently stored clauses, or erase a stored clause. It succeeds when the empty clause is stored. Its clause space is the largest number of simultaneously stored distinct clauses, counting a new conclusion together with its still-stored premises. Proof length and clause width during the derivation are unrestricted.

The question is about general resolution, allowing a retained clause to be reused in arbitrarily many inferences. PSPACE membership is known; the unresolved target is whether the full problem is PSPACE-hard. Satisfiable inputs have no refutation and are no-instances for every finite \(s\).
why: The target asks whether predicting the minimum memory needed by a resolution proof is as hard as arbitrary polynomial-space computation. This would sharpen the distinction between checking a supplied logical derivation and determining whether any derivation fits a memory budget. It also tests how unrestricted reuse of learned information changes the complexity landscape beyond tree-like proof search.
status_note: Open in Nordström (2013), §3.4 Open Problem 3; PSPACE membership is stated there, while general clause-space PSPACE-hardness is asked. On 16 September 2026 this review checked the configuration model, the tree-resolution paper and the source account of the withdrawn total-space claim. The 2021 Buss–Nordström handbook still describes space-decision PSPACE-completeness as likely. The inspected 2023 Papamakarios–Razborov comparisons address different proof-measure relationships and do not classify this exact threshold language. A bounded later-work search found no applicable resolution. This is a source-backed open status with later checks, not an exhaustive certification that no result exists. The acceptance target uses unrestricted input width, binary s and separate inference/erasure steps as specified.

progress.text: Hertel and Urquhart prove PSPACE-completeness of the tree-resolution clause-space problem.
The total-space completeness claim from the earlier Hertel–Pitassi conference paper is withdrawn; the 2013 survey records the issue and separately leaves general clause-space completeness open.
The Handbook of Satisfiability chapter still treats PSPACE-completeness of deciding space as likely rather than known.
New comparisons connect regularized space and restricted resolution measures, without classifying the exact general clause-space decision language.

sentences: Resolution clause space counts how many clauses must coexist while a contradiction is derived.
The selected decision problem takes an arbitrary CNF formula and a binary space budget and asks whether any general resolution refutation fits that budget.
Intermediate clauses may be reused and proof length is unrestricted.
The problem is known to lie in PSPACE, while the established tree-like completeness result does not settle hardness for general resolution.
A classification would explain the computational difficulty of predicting the intrinsic memory needed for proof search.

definitions:
A Boolean variable takes a value in \(\{0,1\}\). A literal is a variable \(x_i\) or its negation \(\neg x_i\). A clause is a finite set of literals, interpreted as their disjunction, and a conjunctive normal form formula, or CNF, is a finite set of clauses interpreted as their conjunction. Repeated literals and repeated clauses in an input list are identified. A clause containing both signs of a variable is permitted and is always true. The empty clause \(\bot=\varnothing\) is always false; a formula with no clauses is always true.

Variables are labeled by positive binary integers in the input. Let \(V(F)\) be the finite set of variables actually occurring in \(F\), and let \(n=|V(F)|\). All proof clauses use only variables in \(V(F)\). Relabeling these variables consecutively is harmless and does not provide extra information. No extension variables or extension axioms are allowed. The formula is given as an explicit list of literal lists, with a sign bit and binary variable label for each literal and delimiters for lists. Include the binary representation of \(s\) and a delimiter separating the two components. The input length \(N\) is the total number of bits. Any fixed conventional self-delimiting encoding of this format is allowed; these explicit encodings are polynomial-time interconvertible. Malformed encodings are no-instances.

A memory configuration \(\mathcal C\) is a finite set of clauses over \(V(F)\). A proof is a finite sequence \(\pi=(\mathcal C_0,\ldots,\mathcal C_T)\) with \(\mathcal C_0=\varnothing\). Each transition applies exactly one of the following operations.

Input download: for a clause \(C\in F\), replace \(\mathcal C\) by \(\mathcal C\cup\{C\}\). The full input formula remains available in a read-only source, but its clauses can be used as inference premises only after being downloaded. Downloaded clauses count toward space just like derived clauses.

Resolution: choose stored clauses \(C,D\in\mathcal C\) and a variable \(x\) such that \(x\in C\) and \(\neg x\in D\). Add the clause
\[R=(C\setminus\{x\})\cup(D\setminus\{\neg x\})\]
to the configuration. Both premises must already be present. Set union removes duplicate literals. Tautological resolvents are allowed. The rule uses one complementary pair, with the displayed set removal defining its exact result.

Weakening: from a stored clause \(C\in\mathcal C\), add any clause \(D\) over \(V(F)\) with \(C\subseteq D\). This is the source's standard optional weakening rule. Weakening is sound and can be eliminated from resolution refutations without increasing clause space, but including it here fixes the proof system explicitly.

Erasure: for a stored clause \(C\in\mathcal C\), replace \(\mathcal C\) by \(\mathcal C\setminus\{C\}\). An erased input clause can later be downloaded again. An erased derived clause can later be obtained again only through legal inferences or because it is also an input clause. There is no free access to a previously erased derived clause.

An inference adds its conclusion without simultaneously deleting its premises. Thus the configuration immediately after the inference is counted before any later erasure. A rule that overwrites a premise with the conclusion in the same step would have a different exact space convention; it is not used in this definition. Adding an already stored clause leaves the set unchanged, and multiple identical copies carry no extra information or storage charge. These conventions follow the general configuration model in Definitions 2.1–2.4 of the source.

A refutation is a proof with \(\bot\in\mathcal C_T\). It need not erase other clauses before it ends. Define
\[\operatorname{Sp}(\pi)=\max_{0\le t\le T}|\mathcal C_t|,\qquad
\operatorname{Sp}(F)=\min_{\pi\text{ refutes }F}\operatorname{Sp}(\pi),\]
with \(\operatorname{Sp}(F)=+\infty\) when no refutation exists. The input is accepted precisely when \(\operatorname{Sp}(F)\le s\). The bound is exact, including its additive constants. For example, space zero never permits the empty clause to be stored, while a formula already containing the empty clause has clause space one.

Clause space counts clauses, regardless of their widths. It is not total space, which counts the sum of literal occurrences in all stored clauses, nor variable space, which counts distinct variables present in memory. It is also not the number of bits used by an algorithm searching for a proof. These are separate resources. The clause-space limit here constrains the proof witness; PSPACE classifies the computational problem of deciding whether such a witness exists.

General resolution permits any stored clause to serve as a premise any number of times before erasure. No tree-like, regular, read-once or input-resolution restriction is imposed. Resolution may use a variable repeatedly along a chain of inferences. There is no bound on \(T\), on the total number of downloads or rederivations, or on any proof clause's width beyond its being a set of literals over \(V(F)\). A short proof is not required as an additional certificate. The input has no satisfiability promise, bounded-width promise, special graph structure or sparsity condition.

PSPACE is the class of languages decided by a uniform deterministic Turing machine that always halts and uses at most \(p(N)\) work-tape bits on inputs of length \(N\), for some fixed polynomial \(p\). The read-only input is not charged to workspace. There is no polynomial-time bound in this class definition. Membership of \(\mathrm{ResClauseSpace}\) requires one such machine for all inputs \(\langle F,s\rangle\), counting \(s\)'s binary encoding as part of \(N\).

A deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction from a language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\) to \(\mathrm{ResClauseSpace}\) is a total function \(f\), computed by one finite deterministic program in time polynomial in \(|z|\), such that
\[z\in L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(z)\in\mathrm{ResClauseSpace}\]
for every binary input string \(z\). It produces one encoded instance, without oracle calls or nonuniform advice. PSPACE-hardness means such a reduction exists for every language \(L\) in PSPACE; the reduction and its polynomial may depend on \(L\). PSPACE-completeness means both this hardness condition and membership in PSPACE. The card asks for this class-completeness assertion, not a proof that PSPACE differs from P.

Scope decision: the imported record joined Open Problems 2 and 3 of the source, concerning total literal space and clause space respectively. On 16 September 2026 the user selected clause space alone, with no extra input-width restriction. This card records that narrowing. The phrase preferably of fixed width in the source motivates a possible stronger hardness theorem but is not an additional acceptance requirement here.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation that \(\mathrm{ResClauseSpace}\), with the exact configuration transitions, binary threshold encoding and unrestricted CNF inputs above, is PSPACE-complete under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions. An affirmative answer must establish both PSPACE membership and hardness with the required uniform reductions and bit-cost bounds. A negative answer must prove that the full completeness assertion is false. Merely placing the language in a smaller complexity class does not refute completeness without the needed separation from PSPACE. A classification for tree-like resolution, total literal space, approximate thresholds or a more restricted class of proofs does not answer the stated question. No numerical benchmark tolerance changes the exact decision predicate. A source citation, experimental proof search or an unformalized reduction is not a substitute for the complete Lean proof.

source_formulation.text: Open Problem 3 asks whether deciding the existence of a resolution refutation with at most a given number of simultaneously retained clauses is PSPACE-complete, preferably even for bounded-width CNF inputs. The adjacent Open Problem 2 asks the separate question for total literal space. The user selected the clause-space question without imposing bounded input width.

context_blocks.text: Resolution derives contradictions by combining clauses. Its memory requirement measures how much derived information must coexist during a proof, even when the proof may be very long. The question asks how difficult it is to determine whether this intrinsic memory requirement fits a supplied budget.

The survey places the general clause-space decision problem in PSPACE and asks whether the corresponding hardness can be proved. This is a decision problem about the existence of an entire proof, rather than about verifying one explicitly supplied proof or measuring one prescribed derivation.

Hertel and Urquhart establish PSPACE-completeness for the tree-resolution space problem. Tree-like derivations restrict reuse of intermediate conclusions. Allowing unrestricted reuse can lower the least required space, so that theorem does not automatically give the claimed hardness for general resolution. Their exact configuration convention also permits deleting parents in the inference step.

The early total-space completeness claim by Hertel and Pitassi was withdrawn after a proof error, as documented in the survey. It concerns a different measure in any event. Neither that withdrawn claim nor the valid tree-like result is recorded as resolving this card.

The 2021 Handbook of Satisfiability chapter still describes PSPACE-completeness of deciding space as a likely classification. It discusses why knowing intrinsic width and space would help interpret proof-search experiments, while distinguishing such proof measures from all of a practical solver's behavior.

Papamakarios and Razborov give later comparisons and trade-offs among several proof measures. Their diagram distinguishes ordinary general clause space from tree-like and regularized quantities, and the comparisons permit polynomial and logarithmic losses. They do not supply an exact-threshold PSPACE-hardness theorem for the language defined here.
